details:
**Coronation by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day, 800**
In Rome on December 25, 800, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne "Emperor of the Romans," and he is usually counted as the first Holy Roman Emperor. Charlemagne had earlier restored Leo after the pope was attacked and accused of crimes by enemies in Rome, and the papacy backed him partly because the Byzantine throne was held by a woman, Empress Irene.

**Einhard and the Vita Karoli Magni**
Einhard was a courtier and scholar who wrote the Life of Charlemagne (Vita Karoli Magni), the main biography of the emperor, and later served his son Louis the Pious. A legend says Einhard eloped with one of Charlemagne's daughters. A later, more anecdotal biography was written by the monk Notker the Stammerer.

**Massacre of Verden and the Saxon Wars**
Charlemagne spent about thirty years conquering and Christianizing the pagan Saxons. In 782 he had about 4,500 Saxon prisoners beheaded at Verden (the "Bloody Verdict of Verden"), and he destroyed the Saxons' sacred pillar or tree, the Irminsul. The Saxon leader Widukind finally submitted and was baptized.

**Alcuin of York and the Carolingian Renaissance**
Alcuin was an English scholar who ran Charlemagne's palace school and led a revival of learning named for Charlemagne's dynasty. Other scholars included Theodulf of Orléans and Paul the Deacon, author of the History of the Lombards. Alcuin retired as abbot of St. Martin at Tours, and Charlemagne's letter De litteris colendis urged monasteries to promote literacy.

**Aachen and the Palatine Chapel**
Charlemagne's capital and favorite residence, in modern western Germany. Its octagonal Palatine Chapel, an early example of a westwork entrance, is the core of today's Aachen Cathedral, where Charlemagne was buried.

**Battle of Roncevaux Pass (778) and The Song of Roland**
After a failed campaign against Zaragoza in Spain, joined by the Muslim governor Sulayman al-Arabi, Charlemagne's rear guard was ambushed by Basques in a pass through the Pyrenees. The death of the commander Roland there became the subject of the Old French epic The Song of Roland, which turns the attackers into Saracens.

**Desiderius and the conquest of the Lombards**
Charlemagne married the daughter of the Lombard king Desiderius, then divorced her and married Hildegard. He besieged Desiderius at Pavia in 773–774, took the title King of the Lombards, and confirmed the Donation of Pepin, his father's grant of land to the papacy.

**Pepin the Short and Charles Martel**
Charlemagne was the son of Pepin the Short, who deposed the last Merovingian king, Childeric III, with the pope's approval and founded the Carolingian dynasty. His grandfather was Charles Martel, "the Hammer," the Mayor of the Palace who defeated a Muslim army at the Battle of Tours in 732.

**Treaty of Verdun (843)**
The treaty in which Charlemagne's grandsons Lothair I, Louis the German, and Charles the Bald divided his empire into three kingdoms after the death of his son Louis the Pious. The division roughly anticipates later France and Germany.

**Carolingian minuscule**
A clear, standardized handwriting script developed by scholars under Charlemagne, associated with Alcuin, to make texts like the Vulgate Bible easier to read and copy. It is the ancestor of modern lowercase letters.

**Missi dominici**
"Envoys of the lord," royal agents sent out in pairs, usually one cleric and one noble, to inspect the provinces, enforce Charlemagne's capitularies (decrees), and check on local counts.

**Harun al-Rashid's elephant, Abul-Abbas**
The Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid sent Charlemagne gifts including an elephant named Abul-Abbas and an elaborate water clock, part of diplomatic contacts between the two rulers.

**Spanish March**
A buffer zone of territory south of the Pyrenees that Charlemagne created to protect his empire from the Umayyad emirate of Córdoba in Spain.

**Monetary reform**
Charlemagne replaced the old gold-based coinage with a silver standard based on the pound, shilling, and penny (denier). Offa of Mercia adopted a similar silver penny in England, and the system lasted in Britain until decimalization.

**Capitulary for the Jews and other capitularies**
Capitularies were Charlemagne's written decrees. The Capitulary for the Jews is attributed to him and restricted Jewish moneylending, while the Capitulare de villis regulated the management of his royal estates.
